content: 1. The stratigraphy of the Saxon homeland, located around Bremen/Weser in present-day Lower Saxony, provides more detailed archaeological layers for the first millennium AD than those found in England or Poland. This region was primarily inhabited by the Chauci and Bructeri Saxon tribes, who were engaged in conflicts with the Romans during the reign of Augustus (31 BC–14 AD). 2. Germanic tribes, including not only the Anglo-Saxons and Frisians but also the Franks, had been competing with Rome for control of the British Isles since the 1st century BC. The Saxons began their incursions into Britain as early as this period, often clashing with the Romans, who may have employed Germanic Franks as auxiliary forces. 3. The La Tène art styles, as described by Hines (1996), were dominant in the pottery of the Saxons. The powerful La Tène Celts, led by King Addedomaros (also known as Aththe-Domaros) of Camulodunum, were among the most significant rulers of this era. 4. A coin of King Maues, dated to the 2nd century BCE, features a jubilant elephant holding a wreath on the obverse, symbolizing victory. The Greek inscription reads Great King of Kings Maues, while the reverse depicts the seated King Maues with a Kharosthi inscription stating the same title. 5. The Antikythera mechanism, a 2nd-century BCE device, contained at least 30 interlocking gear wheels and numerous astronomical inscriptions. Before its discovery on the seabed, it was used to calculate and display the movements of the Sun, Moon, and possibly planets, as well as to predict future eclipse dates. 6. The Winged Nike of Samothrace, carved from Parian marble around 190 BCE, was discovered in 1863 on the island of Samothrace by Charles Champoiseau's archaeological expedition. It is a masterpiece of Hellenistic sculpture. 7. Cleopatra II of Egypt ruled from approximately 175 BCE until her death in 116 BCE. Her reign was marked by significant political and familial turmoil. 8. The Chinese mathematician Liu Hui, during the Three Kingdoms era (220–280 CE), described a sea island survey diagram, showcasing advanced mathematical and surveying techniques. 9. The Jastorf (La Tène) culture, known for its bronze and iron technology, left behind rich archaeological evidence, including structures in downtown Bremen. 10. A 3rd-century BCE dioptra, an astronomical and surveying instrument, was used to measure angles with precision. Finds from this period suggest significant activity in the city from the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, with pottery and coins ceasing to appear after the 2nd century BCE. 11. Edzná, a Mayan archaeological site in northern Campeche, Mexico, was inhabited as early as 400 BCE. The Gran Acropolis is a prominent feature of the site. 12. Construction of the Parthenon in Athens began in 447 BCE and was completed in 438 BCE, with decorative work continuing until 432 BCE. Herodotus wrote that the Temple of Heracles served as a refuge for runaway slaves, who were protected by sacred marks. 13. Croesus, king of Lydia from 560 BCE until his defeat by Cyrus the Great in 546 BCE, issued gold-silver alloy coins. Evidence suggests he may have been burned to death, as depicted on pottery from the period. 14. Sappho of Eresos, a renowned poet, is often depicted holding a lyre and plectrum, symbolizing her contributions to music and literature. 15. An amulet from 800–612 BCE was used to ward off plagues. Esarhaddon, who ruled Assyria from 681–669 BCE, is depicted on a stone stele narrating his restoration of Babylon around 670 BCE. This artifact is now housed in the British Museum. 16. The Nimrud lens, a plano-convex rock-crystal artifact from 750–710 BCE, was discovered in the Assyrian palace of Nimrud by Austen Henry Layard. It may have been used as a magnifying lens or for decorative purposes. 17. The Dipylon Vase, dating to the late Geometric or early Archaic period (circa 750 BCE), features a prothesis scene, depicting the exposure of the dead and mourning rituals. 18. A low-relief from the palace of Sargon II at Dur Sharrukin (modern Khorsabad, Iraq), dated to 716–713 BCE, depicts scenes of Assyrian life and governance. 19. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, dated to 842 BCE, shows King Jehu of Israel bowing before the Assyrian king. This artifact highlights the tribute sent by the Kingdom of Israel and Phoenician cities to Assyria. 20. Carthage, founded in 814 BCE, has been radiocarbon-dated to between 835–800 BCE, aligning with historical accounts by Flavius Josephus and Timaeus. 21. The 10th century BCE corresponds to the period between 3000 and 2900 years before the present (b2k).
